claim: Interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) is a lineage determining transcription factor in hematopoiesis and master regulator of dendritic cells (DC).
source: Interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) is a lineage determining transcription factor in hematopoiesis and master regulator of dendritic cells (DC), an important immune cell for immunity and tolerance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the introduction section.

claim: IRF8 is prominently upregulated in DC development by autoactivation.
source: IRF8 is prominently upregulated in DC development by autoactivation and controls both DC differentiation and function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).

claim: A novel long non-coding RNA is transcribed from the +32 kb enhancer downstream of Irf8 transcription start site and expressed specifically in mouse plasmacytoid DC (pDC), referred to as lncIrf8.
source: Here, we identified a novel long non-coding RNA transcribed from the +32 kb enhancer downstream of Irf8 transcription start site and expressed specifically in mouse plasmacytoid DC (pDC), referred to as lncIrf8.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through RNA-seq data in Figure 1A.

claim: The lncIrf8 locus interacts with the Irf8 promoter.
source: The lncIrf8 locus interacts with the lrf8 promoter and shows differential epigenetic signatures in pDC versus classical DC type 1 (cDC1).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by Capture-C data in Figure 1B.

claim: The lncIrf8 locus shows differential epigenetic signatures in pDC versus classical DC type 1 (cDC1).
source: The lncIrf8 locus interacts with the lrf8 promoter and shows differential epigenetic signatures in pDC versus classical DC type 1 (cDC1).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data in Figure 1A and Figure 2A.

claim: A sequence element of the lncIrf8 promoter, but not lncIrf8 itself, is crucial for mouse pDC and cDC1 differentiation.
source: Interestingly, a sequence element of the lncIrf8 promoter, but not lncIrf8 itself, is crucial for mouse pDC and cDC1 differentiation, and this sequence element confers feedback inhibition of Irf8 expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated by lncIrf8 promoter KO experiments in Figure 2 and lncIrf8 overexpression/rescue experiments in Figure 4.

claim: The lncIrf8 promoter element confers feedback inhibition of Irf8 expression.
source: Interestingly, a sequence element of the lncIrf8 promoter, but not lncIrf8 itself, is crucial for mouse pDC and cDC1 differentiation, and this sequence element confers feedback inhibition of Irf8 expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated by CRISPR activation and interference experiments in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In DC development, Irf8 autoactivation is first initiated by flanking enhancers and then controlled by feedback inhibition through the lncIrf8 promoter element in the +32 kb enhancer.
source: Taken together, in DC development Irf8 autoactivation is first initiated by flanking enhancers and then second controlled by feedback inhibition through the lncIrf8 promoter element in the +32 kb enhancer.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Irf8 knockout mice show abnormal development of classical DC type 1 (cDC1) and plasmacytoid DC (pDC).
source: Irf8 knockout mice show abnormal development of classical DC type 1 (cDC1) and plasmacytoid DC (pDC) (Durai et al., 2019; Schiavoni et al., 2002; Sichien et al., 2016; Tsujimura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Irf8 is prominently upregulated during DC development by autoactivation.
source: Irf8 is prominently upregulated during DC development by autoactivation (Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015), yet how Irf8 autoactivation is controlled and eventually limited, and the epigenetic mechanisms involved is largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Irf8 expression in hematopoietic cells is induced and maintained by enhancers located at –50 kb, +32 kb, +41 kb and +56 kb relative to Irf8 transcription start site (TSS).
source: Irf8 expression in hematopoietic cells is induced and maintained by enhancers located at –50 kb,+32 kb,+41 kb and +56 kb relative to Irf8 transcription start site (TSS) (Anderson et al., 2021; Bagadia et al., 2019; Durai et al., 2019; Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2021; Schönheit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: DC develop from hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) via successive steps of lineage commitment and differentiation.
source: DC develop from hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) via successive steps of lineage commitment and differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: HSC develop into multipotent progenitors (MPP) that are committed to DC restricted common DC progenitors (CDP) and differentiate into classic DC (cDC) type 1 and type 2 (cDC1 and cDC2, respectively) and pDC.
source: More specifically, HSC develop into multipotent progenitors (MPP) that are committed to DC restricted common DC progenitors (CDP) and differentiate into classic DC (cDC) type 1 and type 2 (cDC1 and cDC2, respectively) and pDC (Anderson et al., 2021; Cabeza-Cabrerizo et al., 2021; Ginhoux et al., 2022; Nutt and Chopin, 2020; Rodrigues and Tussiwand, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: pDC were recently shown to develop from lymphoid progenitors.
source: pDC were recently also shown to develop from lymphoid progenitors (Dress et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2018; Rodrigues and Tussiwand, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Differential expression of Irf8 regulates DC and monocyte specification in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Differential expression of Irf8 regulates DC and monocyte specification in a dose-dependent manner (Cytlak et al., 2020; Murakami et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Irf8 expression starts at the CDP stage, and is high in pDC and cDC1.
source: Irf8 expression starts at the CDP stage, and is high in pDC and cDC1, which is attributed to the autoactivation of Irf8 during DC subsets specification (Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: IRF8 can act as a transcriptional activator or repressor in hematopoiesis by interacting with different partner TF and binding to specific DNA sequences.
source: Interestingly, IRF8 can act as a transcriptional activator or repressor in hematopoiesis by interacting with different partner TF and binding to specific DNA sequences (Tamura et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: IRF8 binds to its own promoter in DC differentiation, which is considered as the autoactivation capacity of Irf8.
source: As an activator, IRF8 binds to its own promoter in DC differentiation, which is considered as the autoactivation capacity of Irf8 (Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: IRF8 interacts with partner TF, such as PU.1, to initiate Irf8 autoactivation at the CDP stage.
source: For instance, IRF8 interacts with partner TF, such as PU.1, to initiate Irf8 autoactivation at the CDP stage (Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: IRF8 inhibits C/EBPα activity in neutrophil differentiation.
source: Inversely, IRF8 inhibits C/EBPα activity in neutrophil differentiation (Kurotaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: IRF8 represses C/EBPβ to generate and maintain DC lineage-specific enhancer landscapes.
source: IRF8 also represses C/EBPβ to generate and maintain DC lineage-specific enhancer landscapes (Bornstein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: IRF8 is important for the Myc-Mycl transition in DC differentiation.
source: In addition, IRF8 is important for the Myc-Mycl transition in DC differentiation (Anderson lll et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: IRF8 represses Myc expression in progenitors, while IRF8 at high levels interacts with PU.1 and drives Mycl expression.
source: IRF8 represses Myc expression in progenitors, while IRF8 at high levels interacts with PU.1 and drives Mycl expression (Anderson lll et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: During DC differentiation, the Irf8 gene locus shows high epigenetic dynamics, including histone modifications and TF binding identified by ChIP-seq.
source: During DC differentiation, the Irf8 gene locus shows high epigenetic dynamics, including histone modifications and TF binding identified by ChIP-seq (Chauvistré and Seré, 2020; Durai et al., 2019; Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015), chromatin accessibility measured by ATAC-seq (Kurotaki et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), and three-dimensional chromatin structure remodeling determined by chromosome conformation capture (3 C) (Kurotaki et al., 2022; Schönheit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Irf8 is flanked by multiple enhancers at –50 kb, +32 kb, +41 kb, and +56 kb that regulate Irf8 expression in hematopoietic cells.
source: Notably, Irf8 is flanked by multiple enhancers at –50 kb,+32 kb,+41 kb, and +56 kb that regulate Irf8 expression in hematopoietic cells (Anderson et al., 2021; Murakami et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The four Irf8 flanking enhancers were found to be driven by PU.1, BATF3, E proteins and Runt-related transcription factor (RUNX)-core binding factor beta (CBFβ) (RUNX-CBFβ), respectively.
source: These four enhancers were found to be driven by PU.1, BATF3, E proteins and Runt-related transcription factor (RUNX)-core binding factor beta (CBFβ) (RUNX-CBFβ), respectively (Bagadia et al., 2019; Durai et al., 2019; Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2021; Schönheit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: PU.1 regulates chromatin remodeling between the –50 kb enhancer and the Irf8 promoter in myeloid differentiation.
source: In this study PU.1 was found to regulate chromatin remodeling between the –50 kb enhancer and the Irf8 promoter in myeloid differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referring to work by Schönheit et al.

claim: IRF8 promotes chromatin activation in DC progenitors leading to cDC lineage-specific gene expression.
source: In this study, reorganization of chromatin conformation at DC-specific gene loci was observed during cDC differentiation, and IRF8 was found to promote chromatin activation in DC progenitors leading to cDC lineage-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referring to work by Kurotaki et al., 2022.

claim: De novo transcript assembly of RNA-seq data detected two previously unknown transcripts without coding potential downstream of Irf8: a pDC specific lncRNA (Tcons_00190250, lncIrf8) and a cDC1 specific lncRNA (Tcons_00190258).
source: We performed de novo transcript assembly of the RNA-seq data and detected two previously unknown transcripts without coding potential downstream of Irf8: a pDC specific lncRNA (Tcons_00190250) in the following referred to as lncIrf8 and a cDC1 specific lncRNA (Tcons_00190258; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: lncIrf8 and Tcons_00190258 show the same expression pattern in pDC and cDC1, respectively, in BM and spleen.
source: lncIrf8 and Tcons_00190258 show the same expression pattern in pDC and cDC1, respectively, in BM and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), as revealed by reanalyzing scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data (Pang et al., 2022; Rodrigues et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, supported by reanalysis of published data.

claim: lncIrf8 is transcribed within an enhancer region located 32 kb downstream of the Irf8 TSS labeled by H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and occupied by DC differentiation-associated TF, such as IRF8 and PU.1.
source: lncIrf8 is transcribed within an enhancer region located 32 kb downstream of the Irf8 TSS labeled by H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and occupied by DC differentiation-associated TF, such as IRF8 and PU.1 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lncIrf8 region is largely devoid of H3K9me3, indicating an open chromatin configuration in DC.
source: This region is largely devoid of H3K9me3, a chromatin modification frequently associated with heterochromatin, indicating an open chromatin configureuration in DC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cDC1 the prominent ATAC-seq and IRF8 peaks mark the cDC1 specific +32 kb enhancer.
source: In cDC1 the prominent ATAC-seq and IRF8 peaks mark the cDC1 specific +32 kb enhancer (Durai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2A, with reference to Durai et al., 2019.

claim: In pDC the ATAC-seq peak is smaller and shifted further towards downstream but aligns well with the valley in the prominent H3K27ac peak, marking the lncIrf8 promoter.
source: In pDC the ATAC-seq peak is smaller and shifted further towards downstream but aligns well with the valley in the prominent H3K27ac peak. This ATAC-seq peak marks the lncIrf8 promoter and aligns with p300 (Durai et al., 2019) and H3K4me3 (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Irf8 promoter shows multiple interactions with regions spanning up to ~100 kb upstream and downstream of Irf8.
source: The Irf8 promoter shows multiple interactions with regions spanning up to ~100 kb upstream and downstream of Irf8 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B by Capture-C data.

claim: In pDC, the Irf8 promoter interactions are stronger with the upstream sequences than with downstream sequences.
source: In pDC, the Irf8 promoter interactions are stronger with the upstream sequences than with downstream sequences (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In cDC1 Irf8 promoter interactions are more confined to the regions downstream of Irf8 compared to MPP, CDP and pDC.
source: In cDC1 Irf8 promoter interactions are more confined to the regions downstream of Irf8 compared to MPP, CDP and pDC (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Upstream and downstream sequences of Irf8 gene are involved in differentially regulating Irf8 expression and controlling the development of pDC and cDC1, respectively.
source: This suggests that upstream and downstream sequences of Irf8 gene are involved in differentially regulating Irf8 expression and controlling the development of pDC and cDC1, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the Capture-C data.

claim: Most of the Irf8 flanking enhancers are located within convergent CTCF binding sites upstream and downstream of the Irf8 gene.
source: Interestingly, most of the Irf8 flanking enhancers (Durai et al., 2019; Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2021; Schönheit et al., 2013) are located within convergent CTCF binding sites upstream and downstream of the Irf8 gene (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B, with references to published enhancer locations.

claim: There are multiple interactions within the Irf8 region without convergent CTCF binding sites, suggesting interactions with Irf8 promoter in a CTCF independent manner.
source: There are also multiple interactions within this region without convergent CTCF binding sites, suggesting interactions with Irf8 promoter in a CTCF independent manner, such as by TF binding, active histone modifications and gene transcription (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Owens et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B, with inference about mechanism.

claim: In pDC H3K27ac at the lncIrf8 promoter is high, but this locus shows less interactions with the Irf8 promoter in pDC compared to CDP, cDC1 and cDC2.
source: Surprisingly, in pDC H3K27ac at the lncIrf8 promoter is high, but this locus shows less interactions with the Irf8 promoter in pDC compared to CDP, cDC1 and cDC2 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In pDC the IRF8 protein occupancy at the lncIrf8 promoter is low and much higher in cDC.
source: In addition, in pDC the IRF8 protein occupancy at the lncIrf8 promoter is low and much higher in cDC (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Durai et al., 2019; Grajales-Reyes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A, with references to published ChIP-seq data.

claim: The most prominent isoform of lncIrf8 comprises exon 2 and 3.
source: Our de-novo transcript assembly of RNA-seq data revealed different isoforms of lncIrf8, with the most prominent isoform comprising exon 2 and 3 (Figure 1A, Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 3' end and 5' end RACE PCR confirmed the anatomy of lncIrf8: two exons, one intron, and a polyA tail.
source: Additionally, 3' end and 5' end RACE PCR confirmed the anatomy of this lncIrf8 isoform: two exons, one intron, and a polyA tail (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: lncIrf8 is not conserved across species.
source: As expected lncIrf8 is not conserved across species (data not shown), which is in line with the general characteristics of lncRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is consistent with general knowledge about lncRNAs.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO abolished lncIrf8 expression during DC differentiation.
source: lncIrf8 promoter KO abolished lncIrf8 expression during DC differentiation compared to control without deletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B by RT-qPCR data.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO severely compromised Irf8 expression during DC differentiation.
source: Surprisingly, Irf8 expression was also severely compromised, which points to a cross-talk of the lncIrf8 promoter element with the Irf8 promoter.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B by RT-qPCR data.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO severely reduced frequencies of pDC and cDC1, while cDC2 were unaffected.
source: Frequencies of pDC and cDC1 were severely reduced, while cDC2 were unaffected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C by flow cytometry data.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO cultures showed a marked increase in strongly adhesive cells compared to control.
source: lncIrf8 promoter KO showed a marked increase in strongly adhesive cells compared to control (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B by microscopy.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO cultures had higher frequencies of Gr1+ monocytes upon spontaneous DC differentiation.
source: lncIrf8 promoter KO cultures had higher frequencies of Gr1+ monocytes (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3I, J) and lower frequencies of all DC subsets CD11c+ DC, pDC, cDC1, and cDC2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–G) compared to control without deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E by flow cytometry data.

claim: cDC1 specific +32 kb enhancer KO abolished lncIrf8 expression and decreased Irf8 expression during DC differentiation.
source: Similar to lncIrf8 promoter KO, cDC1 specific +32 kb enhancer KO abolished lncIrf8 expression and also decreased Irf8 expression during DC differentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: cDC1 +32 kb enhancer KO compromised the frequency of cDC1 in Flt3L directed DC differentiation, while cDC2 were unaffected.
source: The cDC1 +32 kb enhancer KO also compromised the frequency of cDC1 in Flt3L directed DC differentiation, while cDC2 were unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E.

claim: cDC1 +32 kb enhancer KO cultures had higher frequencies of Gr1+ monocytes upon spontaneous DC differentiation.
source: In addition, cDC1 +32 kb enhancer KO cultures had higher frequencies of Gr1+ monocytes upon spontaneous DC differentiation by withdrawal of E2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F) and thus showed a similar phenotype as the lncIrf8 promoter KO upon spontaneous DC differentiation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: In bone marrow, lncIrf8 promoter KO cells mostly differentiated into Gr1+ monocytes, and lower frequencies of all DC subsets were observed on day 7 compared to control.
source: In bone marrow, lncIrf8 promoter KO cells mostly differentiated into Gr1+ monocytes, and lower frequencies of all DC subsets were observed on day 7 for lncIrf8 promoter KO cells compared to control (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A-F by flow cytometry data from transplantation experiments.

claim: In spleen, frequencies of cell populations from lncIrf8 promoter KO and control were similar to bone marrow, including lower frequencies of all DC subsets for lncIrf8 promoter KO.
source: In spleen, frequencies of cell populations from lncIrf8 promoter KO and control were similar to bone marrow, including lower frequencies of all DC subsets for lncIrf8 promoter KO (Figure 3G–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3G-L by flow cytometry data from transplantation experiments.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter KO compromised pDC and cDC1 development both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Thus, lncIrf8 promoter KO compromised pDC and cDC1 development both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: lncIrf8 overexpression had no effects on Irf8 expression during DC differentiation.
source: As expected lncIrf8 expression was markedly increased in plncIrf8-pA infected cells compared to control, while there were no significant differences in Irf8 expression between the two groups during DC differentiation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: lncIrf8 overexpression had no effects on the frequencies of pDC, cDC1, and cDC2.
source: Further, there were no differences in the frequencies of pDC, cDC1, and cDC2 between plncIrf8-pA infected cells and controls (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), indicating that lncIrf8 overexpression has no effect on Irf8 expression and DC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D and E by flow cytometry data.

claim: Re-expression of lncIrf8 in lncIrf8 promoter KO MPP did not rescue pDC and cDC1 development.
source: Yet frequencies of pDC and cDC1 were very low to absent and not rescued by lncIrf8 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H by flow cytometry data.

claim: lncIrf8 has no activity on its own in DC differentiation but rather acts as an indicator for the activation state of sequences within the Irf8 +32 kb enhancer.
source: In a nutshell, lncIrf8 overexpression and rescue had no effects on pDC and cDC1 development. This strongly suggests that lncIrf8 has no activity on its own in DC differentiation but rather acts as an indicator for the activation state of sequences within the Irf8 +32 kb enhancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the overexpression and rescue experiments.

claim: The lncIrf8 promoter comprises a sequence element with impact on pDC and cDC1 development.
source: In addition, the lncIrf8 promoter comprises a sequence element with impact on pDC and cDC1 development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the knockout and overexpression experiments.

claim: Activation of the lncIrf8 promoter by dCas9-VP64 caused a massive increase of lncIrf8 expression at DC differentiation day 0.
source: Activation of the lncIrf8 promoter by dCas9-VP64 caused a massive increase of lncIrf8 expression at DC differentiation day 0 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Activation of the lncIrf8 promoter led to Irf8 upregulations at DC differentiation day 5, 7, and 9 compared to non-targeting control.
source: The activation of the lncIrf8 promoter led also to Irf8 upregulations at DC differentiation day 5, 7, and 9 compared to non-targeting control (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Activation of the lncIrf8 promoter demonstrates the positive impact of the lncIrf8 promoter element on Irf8 expression during DC differentiation.
source: This demonstrates the positive impact of the lncIrf8 promoter element on Irf8 expression during DC differentiation and is in accord with the physical interaction of lncIrf8 and Irf8 promoters by Capture-C (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the CRISPR activation data and Capture-C data.

claim: In lncIrf8-VP64 cells lncIrf8 expression was downregulated at DC differentiation day 5, 7 and 9, while Irf8 expression was upregulated.
source: Intriguingly, in lncIrf8-VP64 cells lncIrf8 expression was downregulated at DC differentiation day 5, 7 and 9, while Irf8 expression was upregulated (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: The downregulation of lncIrf8 expression while Irf8 is upregulated indicates a repressive effect of IRF8 on lncIrf8 promoter.
source: This indicates a repressive effect of IRF8 on lncIrf8 promoter and is in accord with IRF8 binding to the lncIrf8 region by ChIP-seq (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the CRISPR activation data and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The observation of lncIrf8 downregulation with Irf8 upregulation suggests a negative feedback loop of IRF8 on the lncIrf8 promoter during DC differentiation.
source: This observation suggests a negative feedback loop of IRF8 on the lncIrf8 promoter during DC differentiation (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the CRISPR activation data.

claim: Activation of Irf8 promoter by dCas9-VP64 increased Irf8 expression at DC differentiation day 0, 5, 7, and 9, while expression of lncIrf8 was unaffected.
source: Activation of Irf8 promoter by dCas9-VP64 increased Irf8 expression at DC differentiation day 0, 5, 7, and 9, while expression of lncIrf8 was unaffected compared to non-targeting control (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Irf8 promoter activation led to higher pDC frequencies.
source: As expected Irf8 promoter activation led to higher pDC frequencies (Figure 5B and D), and also increased cDC1 frequencies compared to the non-targeting controls (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B and D by flow cytometry data.

claim: Irf8 promoter activation increased cDC1 frequencies compared to non-targeting controls.
source: As expected Irf8 promoter activation led to higher pDC frequencies (Figure 5B and D), and also increased cDC1 frequencies compared to the non-targeting controls (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B and E by flow cytometry data.

claim: lncIrf8 promoter activation by dCas9-VP64 increased cDC1 frequencies, particularly prominent at day 9 of DC differentiation.
source: Importantly, lncIrf8 promoter activation by dCas9-VP64 also increased cDC1 frequencies and this was particular prominent at day 9 of DC differentiation (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B and E by flow cytometry data.

claim: CRISPR activation of the lncIrf8 and Irf8 promoters by dCas9-VP64 suggest a negative feedback loop of Irf8 for pDC and cDC1 development.
source: Taken together our CRISPR activation of the lncIrf8 and Irf8 promoters by dCas9-VP64 suggest a negative feedback loop of Irf8 for pDC and cDC1 development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the CRISPR activation experiments.

claim: Targeted repression of the Irf8 promoter decreased Irf8 expression but massively increased lncIrf8 expression.
source: Targeted repression of the Irf8 promoter decreased Irf8 expression as expected but massively increased lncIrf8 expression compared to non-targeting control (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: The massive increase in lncIrf8 expression upon Irf8 promoter repression is in line with Irf8 impacting lncIrf8 expression by a negative feedback loop.
source: This is very much in line with Irf8 impacting lncIrf8 expression by a negative feedback loop.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the CRISPR interference data.

claim: Positioning the dCas9-KRAB repressor in the lncIrf8 promoter led to downregulation of both Irf8 and lncIrf8 expression.
source: Positioning the dCas9-KRAB repressor in the IncIRF8 promoter led to downregulation of both Irf8 and lncIrf8 expression, which confirms the lncIrf8 promoter element acting on the Irf8 promoter (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Targeted repression of the Irf8 promoter severely compromised development of all DC subsets, including pDC, cDC1, and cDC2.
source: Interestingly, targeted repression of the Irf8 promoter severely compromised development of all DC subsets, including pDC, cDC1, and cDC2, compared to non-targeting controls and yielded CD11c+ cells with progenitor-like spherical morphology (Figure 6B and D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B, D-F by flow cytometry and microscopy data.

claim: Targeted repression of the lncIrf8 promoter compromised pDC and cDC1 development.
source: In addition, targeted repression of the lncIrf8 promoter (lncIrf8-KRAB) also compromised pDC and cDC1 development (Figure 6B, D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B, D and E by flow cytometry data.

claim: The result of lncIrf8 promoter repression is very similar to the lncIrf8 promoter KO.
source: This result is very similar to the lncIrf8 promoter KO analyzed above (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a comparison stated in the results.

claim: Irf8 regulates its own expression by a negative feedback loop acting on the Irf8 +32 kb enhancer to limit Irf8 autoactivation.
source: All these findings support a model of Irf8 regulating its own expression by a negative feedback loop acting on the Irf8 +32 kb enhancer to limit Irf8 autoactivation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on all the experimental data.

claim: Irf8 expression starts in CDP and further increases in pDC and cDC1, with particularly high expression in pDC.

source: In conclusion, by analyzing the gene expression and epigenetic profiles of the Irf8 locus, we identified an enhancer element marked by lncIrf8 that regulates Irf8 and controls DC differentiation through a negative feedback loop.
